```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(ggplot2)
  library(knitr)
})

kOutputDir <- file.path("..", "output", "z282")

ReadOutput <- function(name) {
  path <- file.path(kOutputDir, name)
  if (!file.exists(path)) {
    stop(
      "The analysis output is missing: ", path, "\n",
      "Run scripts/09_z282_harmonisation.R first. ",
      "See the section 'Reproducing this'."
    )
  }
  read.csv(path, check.names = FALSE)
}

OutputImage <- function(name) {
  file.path(kOutputDir, name)
}

kArmOrder <- c("local", "central", "automated", "automated shared")

Arm <- function(frame) {
  frame$analysis <- factor(frame$analysis, levels = kArmOrder)
  frame[order(frame$analysis), ]
}

design <- ReadOutput("design.csv")
verdicts <- ReadOutput("claim_verdicts.csv")
```

## Introduction

Macchia et al. reported a multicentre harmonisation study of a six-colour flow
cytometry panel for naive and memory T cell immunomonitoring [1]. Thirteen
operators at five centres stained and acquired the same six samples on seven
instruments. The deposit contains the raw FCS files, the operator analyses, and
the results from one reference operator who re-analysed all 234 files in Kaluza.
Two materials were used: frozen PBMC stained across three days and whole blood
stained on one day.

This report reproduces the paper's acceptability thresholds and Z-score
indicators from the deposit, then adds two automated analysis arms. One arm
applies a single gating rule to every file. The second arm applies the same rule
but uses the median of each operator's own fitted cuts per marker and per
material.

```{r}
#| label: design

kable(design, caption = "The deposit, counted from the file names and from the attached spreadsheet.")
```

```{r}
#| label: operators

kable(
  ReadOutput("operators.csv"),
  caption = "Every operator, the centre they work in, the instrument they used and its model.",
  col.names = c("Operator", "Centre", "Instrument", "Instrument model")
)
```

## Methods

### The dataset

FlowRepository FR-FCM-Z282 contains files from thirteen operators at five
centres. The operators stained and acquired the same six samples on seven
instruments. Two materials were used: frozen PBMC and whole blood. The deposit
holds 234 files. Each operator contributes 18 files, which is two materials,
three vials and three rounds. The frozen PBMC replicates were stained on three
separate days, so they are an interassay measure. The whole blood replicates
were stained on one day and are an intra-assay measure. One reference operator
re-analysed all 234 files in Kaluza.

### Preprocessing

The channel is resolved per file, in two passes. The first pass reads the marker
name the operator typed. The second pass falls back on the fluorochrome, through
`gating/z282_panel.csv`.

Compensation state varies across the deposit. Most Becton Dickinson exports
carry a matrix with `APPLY COMPENSATION` set to `TRUE`, so the values are
already compensated. The Kaluza exports carry `$SPILLOVER` and no such keyword,
so the matrix still has to be applied. Eighteen files carry no matrix at all.

The measurement range is 262,144 on the Becton Dickinson instruments, 1,048,576
on the Gallios, and 1,024 on the eighteen files that one operator exported
already scaled. Every cut is fitted inside one file or inside one operator.

### Gating

The density minimum is the rule of first resort. A two component mixture is the
fallback for CCR7 and CD45RA, which are continuous.

The automated arm applies one rule to all 234 files. It reads no operator's
result and no reference value, and it fits every cut on the file it gates, which
is what an openCyto template does. The automated shared arm applies the same
rule with one change. It takes the median of an operator's own fitted cuts, per
marker and per material, and gates every file of that operator at that one
value.

A file that cannot be gated is reported and dropped, not filled in.

### Statistics

The twenty claims are encoded from the paper with the sentence each came from.
The paper sets acceptability thresholds at CV below 0.20, bias below 0.20 and
ICC above 0.75. Z-score performance is measured against the reference
distribution. A score is unsatisfactory at 3 and questionable between 2 and 3.

The reference operator is treated as Op_M, the letter used in the paper. The
deposit is de-identified with a randomised operator code, and nothing in the
deposit confirms the match.

### Software

The analysis runs in R. Every package version is pinned in the container.

## Results

### Channel resolution and gating

A single template channel name cannot cover this deposit. Three makers name the
same detector three ways. Becton Dickinson writes `PerCP-Cy5-5-A`, one operator
configured the same analyser by laser and filter and it writes `Blue 670 LP-A`,
and Beckman Coulter writes `FL4-A`. The sixth colour is not the same reagent in
the two materials. It is the LIVE/DEAD Near-IR viability dye in the frozen PBMC
panel and anti-CD45 in the whole blood panel, and both sit in the same detector.
Some operators left the marker field empty, so those files carry a detector name
and nothing else.


#### A duplicated acquisition in the deposit

```{r}
#| label: repeats

repeats <- ReadOutput("repeated_acquisitions.csv")
kable(
  repeats,
  caption = "Files that share an acquisition date, a start time and a GUID with another file.",
  col.names = c("File", "Operator", "Material", "Vial", "Round", "Date", "Time",
                "Events")
)
```

These files carry different names and different checksums, and yet their FCS
headers name the same acquisition. The design counts them as separate
replicates, so a repeatability measure computed over them understates the
spread, because two of the three replicates are one measurement exported twice.

### The paper's claims, from the deposit alone

Every claim in this section is answered from the local arm and the central arm.
The automated arms take no part in it.

```{r}
#| label: interoperator-counts

kable(
  Arm(ReadOutput("interoperator_counts.csv")),
  caption = "How many of the fifteen parameters meet each acceptability threshold. The paper sets CV below 0.20, bias below 0.20 and ICC above 0.75.",
  col.names = c("Arm", "Material", "Parameters", "CV acceptable",
                "Bias acceptable", "ICC acceptable"),
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| label: interoperator-cv-figure
#| fig-cap: "Interoperator coefficient of variation, per parameter. The dashed line is the paper's acceptability threshold of 0.20."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("interoperator_cv.png"))
```

```{r}
#| label: interoperator-icc-figure

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("interoperator_icc.png"))
```

```{r}
#| label: intraoperator-counts

kable(
  Arm(ReadOutput("intraoperator_counts.csv")),
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Repeatability within one operator. Each arm holds 195 measurements, which is 13 operators by 15 parameters.",
  col.names = c("Arm", "Material", "Measurements", "Above 0.20", "Median CV",

  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| label: z-counts

kable(
  Arm(ReadOutput("z_counts.csv")),
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Operator performance as a Z-score against the reference distribution. A score is unsatisfactory at 3 and questionable between 2 and 3.",
  col.names = c("Arm", "Material", "Measurements", "Unsatisfactory",

  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| label: z-figure
#| fig-cap: "Every operator and every parameter. Red is an overestimate against the reference value and blue is an underestimate."

```

```{r}
#| label: verdicts

kable(
  verdicts[, c("claim_id", "short_name", "expected", "observed", "verdict")],
  caption = "Every claim the paper makes from the flow data, tested against the deposit.",
  col.names = c("Claim", "What the paper says", "Expected", "Measured",
                "Verdict")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: verdict-counts

kable(
  as.data.frame(table(verdicts$verdict)),
  caption = "How the twenty claims came out.",
  col.names = c("Verdict", "Claims")
)
```

Several claims reproduce to the digit. The intraoperator maximum CV in frozen
PBMC comes out at 1.32 local against 0.75 central, and the median at 0.13
against 0.14. The Z-score counts also land exactly. No score is unsatisfactory
in the central analysis, one is in local frozen PBMC and 49 are in local whole
blood.

The two exact matches come from indicators computed from the paper's own
definitions applied to the paper's own numbers. An exact match shows the
definitions were read correctly before anything else was measured. The counts
that miss by one or two come from the acceptability tables. The paper does not
state whether a parameter exactly at a threshold counts as acceptable, and a
difference of one parameter in fifteen follows from that choice alone.

#### Disagreement between the deposit and the paper

Claim 4 differs by three parameters. The paper reports bias acceptable for 7 of
15 parameters in locally analysed whole blood, and this analysis finds 10. Claim
18 also differs. The paper puts 63.9 percent of the naive and memory variance in
the first two principal components, and this analysis finds a higher figure.

```{r}
#| label: pca

kable(
  ReadOutput("pca_summary.csv"),
  digits = 1,
  caption = "Principal components on the centrally analysed whole blood values.",
  col.names = c("Group", "Variables", "Observations",
                "Variance in the first two components, percent")
)
```

The paper centres and scales its data within each donor and each sample type
before it runs the decomposition, while this analysis scales across the whole
set. The difference in the reported variance follows from that choice, and it is
a difference in method rather than in the data.

### Two automated arms

The second arm exists because the first one showed that per-file cuts follow day
to day drift. A cut fitted once on the pooled cohort avoids changing a frequency
for a reason that is not biology.

```{r}
#| label: shared-cuts

shared <- ReadOutput("shared_cuts.csv")
kable(
  head(shared[order(shared$operator, shared$material, shared$marker), ], 12),
  digits = 2,
  caption = "The first twelve shared cut points. Each one is the median of that operator's own per file cuts, on that operator's own logicle scale.",
  col.names = c("Operator", "Material", "Marker", "Cut")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: distribution-figure
#| fig-cap: "The fifteen frequencies by arm. Every box holds the operator and donor means of one arm."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("distribution_by_arm.png"))
```

```{r}
#| label: intraoperator-figure
#| fig-cap: "Repeatability within an operator, by arm. The dashed line is the acceptability threshold of 0.20."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("intraoperator_cv.png"))
```

### Comparison of the four arms

```{r}
#| label: dispersion

kable(
  Arm(ReadOutput("dispersion_by_arm.csv")),
  digits = 3,
  caption = "The median coefficient of variation across operators, pooled over the fifteen parameters and the three donors.",
  col.names = c("Arm", "Material", "Median CV"),
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

The intraoperator table and the interoperator table answer two different
questions, and the two automated arms separate them. One cut per operator, in
place of one cut per file, cuts the within operator spread by about a third in
frozen PBMC and by a fifth in whole blood. The same change does not improve
agreement between operators. The count of parameters with an acceptable CV and
the count with an acceptable ICC both stay where they were.

```{r}
#| label: icc-after

kable(
  ReadOutput("icc_after_exclusion.csv"),
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Agreement in centrally analysed whole blood, before and after the operators outside a Z of 1.5 are removed.",
  col.names = c("Parameter", "ICC, all operators", "ICC, selected operators")
)
```

The paper runs this same exclusion and reports that two parameters stay below
0.75, and it names them as CD3-CM and CD4-CM. This analysis names the same two.

```{r}
#| label: size

kable(
  Arm(ReadOutput("cv_by_population_size.csv")),
  digits = 3,
  caption = "The median interoperator CV of the three parent populations against the twelve naive and memory subsets.",
  col.names = c("Arm", "Material", "Parent median CV", "Subset median CV"),
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

Precision follows population size in every arm, including both automated ones.
The three parent gates sit on markers with two clear modes. The twelve subsets
sit on CD45RA and CCR7, which have no valley to find.

```{r}
#| label: phenotype

kable(
  ReadOutput("phenotype_by_material.csv"),
  digits = 2,
  caption = "The centrally analysed medians of each material.",
  col.names = c("Material", "CD4 percent of CD3", "CD8 percent of CD3",
                "CD4 over CD8", "CD8 terminally differentiated, percent")
)
```

The paper flags the frozen PBMC preparation as carrying a CD4 over CD8 ratio
below the expected value and a high proportion of terminally differentiated CD8
cells, and the deposit says the same thing. The whole blood samples from the
same study carry a normal ratio, so the anomaly belongs to the frozen
preparation and not to the panel.

## Discussion

### Principal findings

A published harmonisation result reproduces from the deposited spreadsheet. Of
the twenty claims encoded from the paper, most come out as stated, and the two
claims that fix the definitions of every indicator come out to the digit.

The operator effect is now measured. Thirteen analysts working on their own
files disagree by far more than one analyst working on all of them, and the
difference is largest in whole blood, where the material is easiest and the
analysis is therefore the only thing left to vary. The two automated arms
separate repeatability from agreement, which the paper's design cannot do on its
own. A stable boundary fixes the first. Only a shared judgement fixes the
second.

### Weaknesses of the automated arms

Both automated arms sit below the two human arms on every indicator.

Part of the gap is real. A rule that refits a boundary on every file follows the
day to day drift in staining, and a person does not. Part of the gap is built
into the comparison. The Z-score reference is the mean and the spread of the
centrally analysed values, so any arm that differs systematically from the
reference operator scores badly by construction, no matter how self consistent
it is. The frozen PBMC arm carries the worst numbers, and it also carries the
hardest problem. Those replicates were stained on three separate days, so a per
file cut has three days of drift to follow.

### Limitations

It does not show that the paper is right. It shows that the numbers in the paper
follow from the spreadsheet the authors deposited.

Nor does it separate the operator from the instrument. Two centres ran several
operators on one analyser and one operator appears on more than one, so the
design cannot attribute a difference to the person rather than to the machine.
It does not measure the staining either. Every operator stained their own tubes,
so a difference between two operators holds the preparation, the acquisition and
the analysis together. Only the local against central contrast isolates the
analysis, because there the same file is read twice.

The automated arms failed on some files, and those files are dropped. A dropped
file is not a missing measurement at random, because the files that fail are the
ones whose densities do not resolve, which are also the ones a person finds
hardest.

### Further work

The 234 files come from 7 instruments, and the design is unbalanced across them,
so a variance components model with the operator, the instrument and the centre
as separate random effects would say more than the indicators do. It is not run
here.

## Data and code availability

```bash
# Pull this dataset only, 5.8 GB of the 103 GB archive
./sync.sh pull datasets/flowrepository/FR-FCM-Z282

# Derive the committed metadata from the deposit. It runs once, on the host.
uv run --project python python scripts/z282_derive_metadata.py

# Build the container. Every package version is pinned and asserted at build time.
./containers/build.sh

# The analysis
podman run --rm -v "$PWD:/work:z" -w /work everything-flow-cytometry:latest \
  Rscript scripts/09_z282_harmonisation.R

# This report
podman run --rm -v "$PWD:/work:z" -w /work everything-flow-cytometry:latest \
  quarto render reports/z282_harmonisation.qmd
```

The operator results are derived from the spreadsheet the authors attached to
the deposit. They are committed as `gating/z282_operator_results.csv`, so the
claim tests run without the 5.8 GB download. The 234 sample files are needed
only for the two automated arms.

```{r}
#| label: session-info

sessionInfo()
```
